brief: I walked away from a $5M exit. The lifestyle cost, the identity loss, what most founders don't realize about post-acquisition life. A meditation on enough.

slots.subtitle: The hidden cost of selling your company, losing your identity, and finding enough.
slots.preview1: Why a five-million-dollar check feels like loss
slots.preview2: The identity crisis no banker warns about
slots.preview3: Learning to want less after winning big

slots.title: Five million
slots.subtitle: The deal looked perfect. Earnout, equity, a clean handshake. But something felt off.
slots.insight1Body: Investors and advisors measure success in commas; they never ask what you lose between them.
slots.insight2Body: A bigger house and new titles quietly mortgage your mornings, friendships, and creative freedom.
slots.insight3Body: After the ink dries, you become a former founder, a passenger in your own story.
slots.pullQuote: I realized I was about to sell the only thing I could never buy back: my name.

slots.title: Lifestyle inflation
slots.subtitle: More money, more meetings, more maintenance. The exit quietly becomes a second job you never applied for.
slots.insight1Body: You hire managers for your life until calendar white-space disappears behind someone else's priorities.
slots.insight2Body: New zip codes and tax brackets create distance no group chat can fully bridge.
slots.insight3Body: Without constraints, the blank page feels indulgent rather than necessary; you forget how to begin.
slots.pullQuote: I traded my scrappy mornings for a calendar full of people I didn't want to impress.

slots.title: You are not
slots.subtitle: When the company leaves your hands, the mirror asks a question your resume no longer answers.
slots.insight1Body: Founder becomes former founder, and the silence after introductions feels heavier than any pitch.
slots.insight2Body: Board seats and press mentions fade fast; the work itself was the only real credential.
slots.insight3Body: Without a product to ship, you must learn to matter to yourself before you matter to markets.
slots.pullQuote: I walked into a room and nobody needed me. That was the real acquisition.

slots.title: Post-exit grief
slots.subtitle: Advisors celebrate the close; nobody warns you about the Monday morning with no standup, no fire.
slots.insight1Body: Champagne toasts cover a quiet panic that begins the moment the all-hands email goes silent.
slots.insight2Body: Your team becomes someone else's team, and Slack notifications are replaced by an eerie, permanent calm.
slots.insight3Body: The next milestone isn't revenue; it is learning to wake up without a dashboard to check.
slots.pullQuote: They call it a liquidity event. They never tell you how much of yourself gets liquidated.

slots.title: The art of
slots.subtitle: Enough is not a number. It is the moment desire no longer outpaces your own attention.
slots.insight1Body: I sold nothing and gained mornings, long walks, and the right to change my mind.
slots.insight2Body: A lifestyle business that feeds your soul outlasts any earnout that feeds only your ego.
slots.insight3Body: The return on investment I now track is uninterrupted dinners and ideas born from boredom.
slots.pullQuote: I found that enough is not the absence of ambition, but the end of borrowed desire.

slots.title: Build a life
slots.subtitle: Before you sign, audit what remains. Here is the due diligence most founders forget to run.
slots.insight1Body: Write the three daily rituals you refuse to outsource; if the deal kills them, walk.
slots.insight2Body: Do not just forecast cash flow; visualize your calendar, your friendships, and your creative hours.
slots.insight3Body: Negotiate a sabbatical clause or advisory role that preserves identity while you test post-sale life.
slots.pullQuote: The best due diligence is asking whether the person you become can stand the person you were.

slots.ctaBody: Walk away from deals that steal your name. Enough is a choice you make before the offer.
